title: Choose the capital structure and offering exemption
summary: Pick a single-asset syndication, a blind-pool fund or a joint venture, and the exemption the raise relies on: Rule 506(b), Rule 506(c) or, for one capital partner, Section 4(a)(2) alone. Agents test the investor list and the plan against each rule; counsel makes the call before the first investor conversation.

steps.title: Write down the raise in one page
steps.instruction: From the underwriting model and the sponsor's notes, write down the facts every later step tests: one property or a pool of future deals; the equity needed and the minimum check; how many investors, who they are, whether each is accredited, and how the sponsor knows them; whether the sponsor wants to market the deal publicly; whether anyone will be paid for bringing in investors; and the states where investors live. Mark each answer known or assumed. Unknowns become questions for the sponsor, not guesses.
steps.modeBasis: The facts come from the model and the sponsor's notes; an agent assembles them and flags the gaps.

steps.title: List prospects and how each relationship began
steps.instruction: Start from the latest dated copy of build-investor-list's confirmed list, and name the copy used. For each prospect not on it, and only those, the sponsor states when and how the relationship began and what the sponsor knew about the person's finances and investing experience before any offering started. SEC staff treats a pre-existing, substantive relationship as one way, not the only way, to show that offers were not a general solicitation. Pre-existing means formed before the offering began, or through a registered broker-dealer or adviser before it joined the offering; substantive means the sponsor had enough information to evaluate, and did evaluate, the person's financial circumstances and sophistication. A self-certification checkbox alone does not make a relationship substantive.
steps.modeBasis: Only the sponsor knows when and how each relationship formed; an agent can format the list but cannot attest to it.

steps.title: Check whether the interests are securities
steps.instruction: Map the planned interest to the Supreme Court's investment-contract test: an investment of money in a common enterprise with profits to come solely from the efforts of others. Passive investors in a syndication or fund who rely on the sponsor to buy, run and sell the property line up with each element, which is why the exemption steps that follow matter. Write a short note tying each element to the deal terms for counsel, who decides. A joint venture with one active capital partner gets its own test in a later step.
steps.modeBasis: Mapping deal terms to a published test is analysis; the legal conclusion stays with counsel.

steps.title: Test the raise against Rule 506(b)
steps.instruction: Rule 506(b) suits a raise from people the sponsor already knows. Check the plan against it: no general solicitation or advertising by the sponsor or anyone acting for it; any number of accredited investors; no more than 35 non-accredited purchasers in any 90-calendar-day period, each able to evaluate the merits and risks alone or with a purchaser representative. Selling to even one non-accredited investor requires Rule 502(b) disclosure, including financial statements, so note that cost. Flag every prospect without a documented relationship; whether an offer to them would be a general solicitation depends on the facts, so it goes to counsel.
steps.modeBasis: The conditions are written rules applied to the prospect list and the marketing plan.

steps.title: Test the raise against Rule 506(c)
steps.instruction: Rule 506(c) allows public marketing, such as a website or an open webinar, if every buyer is an accredited investor and the sponsor takes reasonable steps to verify each one, even buyers who plainly qualify. Note which verification route fits the investor base: tax forms, recent asset and credit documents, a recent letter from a CPA, attorney, broker-dealer or SEC-registered adviser, or, under the SEC staff position, a minimum investment of at least $200,000 per individual or $1,000,000 per entity with written representations. Once the sponsor has generally solicited, a failed Rule 506(c) offering cannot fall back on Section 4(a)(2).
steps.modeBasis: The conditions and the staff position are published; matching them to the investor base is analysis.

steps.title: Check anyone who will be paid to raise money
steps.instruction: List everyone who will be paid for bringing in investors, including the sponsor's own staff and any outside finder. SEC staff names finders who locate investors for issuers among those who may need broker-dealer registration, and asks whether pay depends on the size or outcome of the deal. The sponsor's own people fall within the issuer safe harbor only if, among other conditions, they receive no commissions or other transaction-based pay. Texas bars paying anyone who solicits Texas investors under Rule 506 unless that person is registered in Texas as a dealer or agent, or as an individual finder paid only to introduce accredited investors. Every paid solicitor is also a bad-actor covered person and is named on Form D.
steps.modeBasis: Comparing the planned pay arrangements with published rules is document work; any doubtful arrangement goes to counsel.

steps.title: List covered persons and screen for bad-actor events
steps.instruction: Rule 506 is unavailable if a covered person has a disqualifying event, so screen before relying on it. From the sponsor and entity documents, list the issuer and its affiliated issuers; directors, executive officers, other officers in the offering, general partners and managing members; holders of 20% or more of the voting equity; promoters; paid solicitors and their principals; and, for a fund, the investment manager. Ask each person to flag any securities-related conviction, injunction, order, bar or suspension. Any yes goes to counsel now: it can rule out Rule 506, and events before September 23, 2013 must still be disclosed to buyers.
steps.modeBasis: Listing covered persons from the documents is document work; each person answers for themselves and counsel reads any yes.

steps.title: Map the fund to an Investment Company Act exclusion
steps.instruction: A fund that invests in securities can be an investment company under the Investment Company Act unless an exclusion applies. Note what the fund will hold: property owned directly or through subsidiaries, interests in other entities, or loans. Then compare the investor plan with the exclusions counsel will weigh: Section 3(c)(1), no more than 100 beneficial owners and no public offering; Section 3(c)(7), qualified purchasers only, such as individuals with at least $5,000,000 in investments; and Section 3(c)(5)(C), for issuers primarily acquiring mortgages, other liens on and interests in real estate. Rule 506 offers are not public offerings because of general solicitation. Form D Item 6 reports the exclusion.
steps.modeBasis: Comparing the planned holdings and investor base with the statute is analysis; counsel chooses the exclusion.

steps.title: Test the joint venture interest and its exemption
steps.instruction: In the Fifth Circuit, which hears appeals from Texas, a general partnership or joint venture interest is ordinarily not a security, because the partner holds real control. It can become one if the agreement leaves the partner little more power than a limited partner, if the partner is too inexperienced to use its powers, or if it depends so heavily on the sponsor's unique skill that it cannot replace the sponsor. If counsel treats the interest as a security, a sale to one sophisticated partner can rely on Section 4(a)(2) alone, with no Form D, but then Texas law needs its own exemption, such as the self-executing private-offering exemptions.
steps.modeBasis: Testing the draft control terms against the court's factors is analysis; counsel makes the call.

steps.title: Decide the structure and exemption with counsel
steps.instruction: Give counsel the one-page profile, build-investor-list's dated list with the answers for prospects not on it, and the notes from the tests above. The sponsor chooses the business structure; counsel chooses the exemption and, for a fund, the Investment Company Act exclusion, and says whether a joint venture interest is a security. Ask for the decision in writing with its conditions: who may be contacted and how, whether non-accredited investors may buy, the verification method under Rule 506(c), and who, if anyone, may be paid to solicit.
steps.modeBasis: Choosing the exemption is a legal judgment for counsel; choosing the structure is the sponsor's business decision.

steps.title: Record the decision and the rules it imposes
steps.instruction: Write the decision into the firm file and turn it into rules for everyone who talks to investors. Under Rule 506(b): no offers on a public website, no ads, no open invitations to events, and no impersonal mass outreach to people outside the documented relationships. Under Rule 506(c): the verification method and the records kept for each buyer. Note the exits: an offering can switch from 506(c) to 506(b) only if no general solicitation occurred and every sale met 506(b), and from 506(b) to 506(c) only before any sale; either switch means amending a Form D already filed.
steps.modeBasis: Turning a written decision into checklists and file entries is document work.
